source.title: Open problems in nuclear structure near drip lines

accepted.question_text: What information about dilute neutron matter and asymmetric nuclear matter can be inferred from finite neutron-rich nuclei near the neutron drip line? In particular, can observed neutron halos and neutron skins be used to extract properties of dilute neutron matter, determine the symmetry energy of asymmetric nuclear matter, and quantify how strongly low-density matter properties are manifested in finite nuclei whose outer neutron density is far below normal nuclear saturation density?
accepted.context_brief: Halo and skin constraints on dilute matter

evidence.quote: Is it possible to extract information on dilute neutron matter from the observed properties of the neutron halo and skin? Can we obtain the symmetry energy of asymmetric nuclear matter? How significantly are these matter properties manifested by finite nuclei? These are still open questions to answer.

accepted.question_text: Do the correlations predicted for dilute nuclear or neutron matter actually occur in finite nuclei, and if so how are they connected to observed finite-nucleus phenomena such as spatial di-neutron correlation in two-neutron-halo nuclei, surface di-neutron correlation in neutron-rich isotopes, and low-density alpha clustering in the Hoyle state of carbon-12? The open problem is to establish whether these finite-nucleus signatures are manifestations of the same exotic low-density correlations expected in dilute matter.

evidence.quote: It is also a non-trivial and open question whether these correlations characteristic to dilute matter can be found in finite nuclei.
It is of crucial importance to investigate possible link between these observations and the exotic correlations in dilute nuclear (neutron) matter.

accepted.question_text: What is the correct microscopic description of nuclei at the neutron or proton drip lines when weak binding, short-range nucleon-nucleon correlations, long-range many-body correlations, and continuum coupling all matter at once? Within that description, does pairing suppress the spatial halo of weakly bound neutrons through an anti-halo effect, and how important are three-body interactions, such as Fujita-Miyazawa-type forces, in determining drip-line structure and isotope limits?
accepted.context_brief: Microscopic drip-line structure and halo physics

evidence.quote: Can these neutrons travel without the collision longer than stable nuclei? We need a microscopic picture of the nucleus at the drip lines, with full account of short-range nucleon-nucleon correlation and long-range many-body correlation in the continuum [18, 19]. Does the paring correlation suppress the halo effect (anti-halo effect) [20, 21]?
Furthermore, the three-body interaction might also play an important role at the drip line.

accepted.question_text: In medium-mass and heavy nuclei at the neutron drip line, where several loosely bound orbitals can accommodate many neutrons and neutron and proton Fermi momenta differ strongly, what new many-body correlations and collective excitation modes should appear? More specifically, does the large neutron-proton asymmetry produce collective motion in which neutrons and protons move partly independently rather than in the predominantly isoscalar manner familiar from stable nuclei?
accepted.context_brief: Collective modes in weakly bound many-body nuclei

evidence.quote: A nucleus at the neutron drip line in the medium- and heavy-mass region may have several loosely bound orbitals which are able to accommodate many neutrons. What kind of many-body correlations and collective modes of excitation can we expect in such circumstances?
Does this lead to independent collective motion of neutrons and protons?

accepted.question_text: How should the Coulomb dissociation of two-neutron-halo nuclei be described when the emitted neutrons are correlated? Unlike one-neutron halo systems, where low-energy electric-dipole strength can often be interpreted as a single-particle transition from a weakly bound orbital to low-energy continuum orbitals, the open problem is to determine the role and form of two-neutron correlations in the dissociation process for halo nuclei with two loosely bound neutrons.

evidence.quote: In nuclei containing two or more loosely bound nucleons, however, the situation is not that simple as the correlation among these nucleons comes into the game. It has been discussed for a long time, but the correlation in the Coulomb dissociation process is still an open issue for two-neutron-halo nuclei [11, 12, 25].

accepted.question_text: What is the physical nature of the pygmy dipole resonance in neutron-rich nuclei, especially as neutron separation energy decreases toward the drip line? The unresolved problem is to determine how collective these low-energy electric-dipole excitations are, what mechanism generates them, and how they connect to the low-energy dipole mode of nuclei containing very weakly bound neutrons, including whether they are primarily a decoupled vibration of the neutron skin, a single-particle excitation of loosely bound neutrons, or a mode strongly shaped by pairing and di-neutron correlations in the low-density neutron skin.

evidence.quote: How collective are the pygmy dipole resonance? What is the mechanism of causing the pygmy resonance? How the pygmy dipole resonance is connected to the low-energy dipole mode which emerges in drip-line containing very weakly bound neutrons. We have not reached a unique answer on the nature of these pygmy excitations.
It is certainly an open problem for nuclear structure theory to make a reliable theoretical prediction and precise description of the excitation modes.

accepted.question_text: How should the nuclear energy density functional be extended so that it can make reliable predictions at the drip lines? This includes explaining the Wigner energy in nuclei with equal neutron and proton numbers near the proton drip line, determining whether isoscalar T = 0 pairing is responsible for that extra binding, and constructing a functional that remains valid despite incomplete knowledge of low-density clustering and high-density many-body interactions, so that empirical data near the drip lines can properly constrain the functional form.
accepted.context_brief: Energy density functional for drip lines

evidence.quote: Despite of recent efforts to improve the energy density functional, it is still far from solid prediction of the drip lines (see Sec. 1).

A major problem at the proton drip line is related to the Wigner energy in N = Z nuclei. It cannot be explained by conventional density functionals and its extension is necessary. There are some arguments that the isoscalar (T = 0) pairing might be responsible for the Wigner energy [32, 33], but it is not conclusive yet.

accepted.question_text: What pairing energy functional should be used in nuclear density functional theory so that pair correlations are described consistently from very low-density neutron matter, where strong-coupling behavior can appear, up to normal saturation density? The open problem is to determine the functional form of the pairing contribution Epair as a function of neutron density, proton density, and pair densities in a way that is accurate enough for drip-line physics.

evidence.quote: Its functional form, Epair[ρn,ρ p, ˜ρn, ˜ρp], is then need to be determined, but it is an open problem currently under discussion [34, 35, 36]. We need an elaborate pairing functional Epair[ρn,ρ p, ˜ρn, ˜ρp] which can cover from the low density limits to the saturation density in order to describe physics at the drip lines.

accepted.question_text: How can time-dependent many-body theory be extended to describe weakly bound nuclei and nuclear reactions in the continuum with the correct asymptotic behavior and pairing dynamics? The unresolved tasks include solving time-dependent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov equations for pair-correlated systems in medium-mass and heavy drip-line nuclei, handling reactions with more than three particles, and resolving the conceptual problem of how to compute exclusive cross sections within time-dependent density functional theory without unphysical cross-channel correlations of the kind known from time-dependent Hartree-Fock.

evidence.quote: Firstly, we need to include the pair correlation in the density-functional approaches, which is essential for description of weakly-bound nuclei in medium- and heavy-mass regions. In other words, we should solve the time-dependent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov (TDHFB) equations which can describe the dynamics of the pair correlated many-body systems on the basis of the pairing functional Epair[ρn,ρ p, ˜ρn, ˜ρp].
However, calculation of the exclusive cross sections have some conceptual open problems we need to solve. This is similar to the famous problem of spurious cross channel correlations in TDHF [40].

accepted.question_text: How can a quasiparticle random phase approximation be developed that simultaneously includes pairing correlations, explicit continuum states, shape deformation, and full self-consistency of all residual fields for nuclei near the drip line? The challenge is to formulate linear response on top of time-dependent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory even though, in the quasiparticle representation, the relevant phase space becomes effectively infinite when continuum orbitals are treated explicitly, and then to build numerical methods and algorithms suitable for large-scale parallel computation and for eventual application to both finite nuclei and inhomogeneous nuclear matter.

evidence.quote: A big open problem is, therefore, to develop the quasiparticle random phase approximation (QRPA) techniques which can include both the pair correlation and the continuum on top of the features mentioned above.

The linear response calculation with full self-consistency and the continuum requires a large-scale numerical effort, for which we need to develop a new methodology and an algorithm suitable for the massive parallel computation.
